spec.cue: The view is wide and soft, with the middle a little sharper, and it runs a little faster than yours. Colours shift toward ultraviolet, so blues and whites look different.

cpd.note: the whole picture at about the typical bee acuity of 0.25 to 0.53 cycles per degree

fov.note: the two eyes together cover about 270 to 300 degrees

BEE.note: UV peak 350 nm (R71), blue 440 nm (R77 and R75 bracket it), green 540 nm (R86 and R89)

saccade.note: app's choice for timing; records give 45 to 135 ms saccades (R145)

rows: Bees see far less detail than people. Their eyes resolve about a quarter of a grating cycle per degree, roughly 1/230 of a person, so the picture is soft.
Bee eyes have three colour classes, ultraviolet, blue and green. Ultraviolet peaks near 340 to 350 nm, blue near 440 nm and green near 540 nm, so the picture shifts toward those colours.
Honeybees see a flicker up to about 200 hertz in bright light, so the picture runs slower than yours and steps as it plays.
Taken together, a bee's two eyes cover nearly all round, about 270 to 300 degrees, with a small blind region behind.
Bees steer by the movement of the world past their eyes, and their head turns quickly from one view to the next.
The soft middle, the glow, the gaze timings and the ultraviolet tint are the app's own choices, drawn from these records but not measured as such.

claims.how: Bee acuity records sit at 0.25 and 0.26 cycles per degree, and the stingless bee at 0.53, so 0.3 lies near the bee middle.
Two group records give 300 and 270 degrees, and 300 is taken as the upper figure of that pair.
Honeybee flicker fusion of about 200 Hz in bright light against 60 Hz for a person gives 60/200 = 0.3; graded i because the record is a receptor-level limit and the ratio is the app's own mapping.

quotes.quote: They found that the highest spatial frequency reliably resolved by the bees was 0.26 cycle deg−1, with no evidence of a difference in acuity between horizontal and vertical gratings.
buff-tailed bumblebees have a resolution threshold of about a quarter of a grating cycle per degree of visual angle.
They resolve a grating of period 3°-4° in daylight
Bees can see ~300° horizontally on the body plane with low spatial resolution for peripheral ommatidia
a very coarse representation of the whole 270° bee eye horizontal field of view
the photoreceptor cells of bees exhibit sensitivity peaks in the ultraviolet (∼350 nm), blue (∼440 nm), and green (∼540 nm) bands
Honeybees' and bumblebees' peak wavelength sensitivity of UV photoreceptors lies at approximately 340 nm
At ca. 200 Hz the FRC drops to 50%.
The temporal resolution of colour vision, determined to be at 100 Hz in free-flying bees through measurements of the flicker-fusion frequency
‘saccades’, when angular velocities of the head reach up to 1500°/sec (see Fig 2C)
Instead, bumblebees appear to use the maximum magnitude of translational optic flow experienced in the frontal visual field.
Generally, the two compound eyes of bees have large visual fields, with a binocular region frontally and dorsally, and only a small blind region below and behind the animal.
In contrast to us, bees can see UV light but not far red.
